title: Ἕκτορος θάνατος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Hector, whose spear has glanced off Achilles’ shield, turns to call Deiphobus for another and finds no one there; he understands that Athena has tricked him, and that the gods have given him up. He draws his sword and rushes in like an eagle, and Achilles meets him behind his great shield, with the light of his spear-point shining like the evening star. Achilles drives the point through Hector’s throat at the one place the borrowed armour of Patroclus leaves bare, and Hector falls. He begs Achilles to give his body back for burial, and Achilles refuses in terms of dogs and raw flesh. Dying, Hector foretells Achilles’ own death at the Scaean Gates, by the hands of Paris and Apollo. Achilles strips the body while the Achaeans crowd round to wound it, then proposes a trial of the city, and drops the thought at once for the sake of unburied Patroclus. He pierces the dead man’s ankles, ties him to the chariot and drags him off, his dark hair trailing in the dust.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἀμπεπαλὼν προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος,
καὶ βάλε Πηλεΐδαο μέσον σάκος οὐδ’ ἀφάμαρτε·
sentences.tr:
ē rha, kai ampepalōn proïei dolichoskion enchos,
kai bale Pēleïdao meson sakos oud’ aphamarte·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and having brandished it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear,
and hit the middle of the shield of Peleus’-son, and did not miss;
sentences.i: So he said, and brandishing it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear, and hit the son of Peleus full in the middle of his shield, and did not miss;
sentences.n: The speaker of the last lines, Hector, now throws; the name is not repeated, and Πηλεΐδαο ‘of Peleus’ son’ is Achilles. ἦ ῥα, καί ‘he spoke, and’ is a stock opening and the English for it stays the same each time. ἀμπεπαλών is the aorist participle of ἀναπάλλω, ‘brandishing’ the spear by swinging it back, and προΐει (‘sent forth’) is the unaugmented imperfect of προΐημι. μέσον σάκος is ‘the middle of the shield’, and ἀφάμαρτε is an unaugmented aorist of ἀφαμαρτάνω ‘miss’.

sentences.t:
τῆλε δ’ ἀπεπλάγχθη σάκεος δόρυ· χώσατο δ’ Ἕκτωρ
ὅττί ῥά οἱ βέλος ὠκὺ ἐτώσιον ἔκφυγε χειρός,
στῆ δὲ κατηφήσας, οὐδ’ ἄλλ’ ἔχε μείλινον ἔγχος.
sentences.tr:
tēle d’ apeplanchthē sakeos dory· chōsato d’ Hektōr
hotti rha hoi belos ōky etōsion ekphyge cheiros,
stē de katēphēsas, oud’ all’ eche meilinon enchos.
sentences.l:
And far off glanced away from the shield the spear; and Hector was incensed
that for him the swift shaft in vain had flown from his hand,
and he stood, downcast, nor had he another ashen spear.
sentences.i: But the spear glanced far away from the shield; and Hector was incensed that his swift shaft had flown from his hand in vain, and he stood downcast, with no other ashen spear.
sentences.n: ἀπεπλάγχθη is the aorist passive of ἀποπλάζω, ‘was knocked off course’, and the spear (δόρυ) is the subject. Line 292 stands in the same words at 14.407, and the English shipped there is reused. κατηφήσας is the aorist participle of κατηφέω, ‘be downcast’, and the shame of a miss is the sense. οὐδ’ ἄλλ’ ἔχε is ‘nor did he have another’: ἔχε is the unaugmented imperfect, and μείλινον ‘ashen’ means a shaft of ash-wood.

sentences.t:
Δηΐφοβον δ’ ἐκάλει λευκάσπιδα μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
ᾔτεέ μιν δόρυ μακρόν· ὃ δ’ οὔ τί οἱ ἐγγύθεν ἦεν.
sentences.tr:
Dēïphobon d’ ekalei leukaspida makron aÿsas·
ēitee min dory makron· ho d’ ou ti hoi engythen ēen.
sentences.l:
And he called Deiphobus of the white shield, shouting loudly;
he was asking him for a long spear; but he was not at all near him.
sentences.i: He called out loudly to white-shielded Deiphobus and asked him for a long spear; but Deiphobus was nowhere near him.
sentences.n: Hector calls his brother Deiphobus, the one he thinks is beside him (Athena in his shape; see 22.227 and following). Δηΐφοβον is the accusative of the name, and λευκάσπιδα ‘of the white shield’ is a fixed epithet in the accusative with it. μακρὸν ἀΰσας ‘shouting loudly’ is a stock phrase, with ἀΰσας the aorist participle of ἀΰω. ᾔτεε is the imperfect of αἰτέω, ‘was asking for’, with two accusatives, μιν ‘him’ and δόρυ ‘a spear’. ὃ δ’ at the start of the next clause is Deiphobus; οὔ τι οἱ ἐγγύθεν ἦεν, ‘was not at all near him’, uses ἦεν, the epic imperfect of εἰμί.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἔγνω ᾗσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: Hektōr d’ egnō hēisin eni phresi phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: And Hector knew in his own wits, and spoke:
sentences.i: Then Hector understood in his own mind, and said:
sentences.n: ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω, ‘knew, understood’; there is no object, and the speech that follows tells what he has understood. ᾗσιν ἐνὶ φρεσί has the possessive ᾗσιν, ‘his own’, in the dative plural with the epic ending -σιν, agreeing with φρεσί, the dative plural of φρένες (‘wits, mind’); ἐνί is the epic form of ἐν. φώνησέν τε ‘and spoke’ prepares the speech.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ μάλα δή με θεοὶ θάνατόνδε κάλεσσαν·
Δηΐφοβον γὰρ ἔγωγ’ ἐφάμην ἥρωα παρεῖναι·
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἐν τείχει, ἐμὲ δ’ ἐξαπάτησεν Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi ē mala dē me theoi thanatonde kalessan·
Dēïphobon gar egōg’ ephamēn hērōa pareinai·
all’ ho men en teichei, eme d’ exapatēsen Athēnē.
sentences.i: “Ah, the gods have truly called me to my death; for I thought the hero Deiphobus was at my side, but he is inside the wall, and it is Athena who has deceived me.
sentences.n: Hector understands that he has been tricked. ὢ πόποι is a cry of dismay, ‘Ah!’, and θάνατόνδε is θάνατον with the ending -δε, ‘to death’. ἐφάμην is the imperfect middle of φημί, ‘I thought, I said to myself’; παρεῖναι ‘to be present’ is the infinitive of πάρειμι. Line 299 sets ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἐν τείχει ‘but he is inside the wall’ against ἐμὲ δ’ ἐξαπάτησεν Ἀθήνη; ὃ is Deiphobus, and ἐξαπάτησεν is the aorist of ἐξαπατάω ‘deceive’. Deiphobus was never there: it was Athena in his shape.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ δὴ ἐγγύθι μοι θάνατος κακός, οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἄνευθεν,
οὐδ’ ἀλέη· ἦ γάρ ῥα πάλαι τό γε φίλτερον ἦεν
Ζηνί τε καὶ Διὸς υἷι ἑκηβόλῳ, οἵ με πάρος γε
πρόφρονες εἰρύατο· νῦν αὖτέ με μοῖρα κιχάνει.
sentences.tr:
nyn de dē engythi moi thanatos kakos, oud’ et’ aneuthen,
oud’ aleē· ē gar rha palai to ge philteron ēen
Zēni te kai Dios huii hekēbolōi, hoi me paros ge
prophrones eiryato· nyn aute me moira kichanei.
sentences.l:
and now evil death is near me, and no longer far away,
nor is there escape; for truly then long ago this was dearer
to Zeus and to the far-shooting son of Zeus, who before
were ready-minded to guard me; but now fate overtakes me.
sentences.i: and now evil death is close to me, no longer far off, and there is no escape; for this, it seems, has long been the more welcome thing to Zeus and to Zeus’ far-shooting son, who before this readily guarded me; but now my fate overtakes me.
sentences.n: Hector reads it as the gods’ long-standing wish. ἐγγύθι and ἄνευθεν are ‘near’ and ‘far off’, and ἀλέη is ‘escape’. ἦ γάρ ῥα πάλαι τό γε φίλτερον ἦεν is ‘for indeed, it seems, this was long since the dearer thing’: τό is his death, φίλτερον the comparative of φίλος, and ῥα marks the sudden realisation. Ζηνί is the dative of Ζεύς in its Ζην- stem, and Διὸς υἷι ἑκηβόλῳ is ‘the far-shooting son of Zeus’, which is Apollo. εἰρύατο is the 3rd plural of ἐρύομαι ‘guard’ (a plain past tense here), and πρόφρονες ‘ready-minded’ is the ready-hearted help they gave once. μοῖρα is ‘fate’ and κιχάνει ‘overtakes’.

sentences.t:
μὴ μὰν ἀσπουδί γε καὶ ἀκλειῶς ἀπολοίμην,
ἀλλὰ μέγα ῥέξας τι καὶ ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
mē man aspoudi ge kai akleiōs apoloimēn,
alla mega rhexas ti kai essomenoisi pythesthai.
sentences.l:
Not at least without a fight and without glory may I perish,
but having done something great, for those yet to come to hear of.”
sentences.i: At least let me not perish without a fight and without glory, but after doing some great deed for men yet to come to hear of.”
sentences.n: Hector asks for a death that will be remembered. μὴ μὰν … ἀπολοίμην is a wish in the optative, ‘may I not perish’. ἀσπουδί (‘without trouble’ in the other place it appears, 8.512) here means ‘without a fight’, and ἀκλειῶς is ‘without glory’, both said of how he will not die. ῥέξας is the aorist participle of ῥέζω ‘do’, and ἐσσομένοισι is the dative plural of ‘those who will be’, so ‘for those yet to come’, with πυθέσθαι ‘to hear, learn’ an infinitive of purpose. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας εἰρύσσατο φάσγανον ὀξύ,
τό οἱ ὑπὸ λαπάρην τέτατο μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε,
οἴμησεν δὲ ἀλεὶς ὥς τ’ αἰετὸς ὑψιπετήεις,
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas eiryssato phasganon oxy,
to hoi hypo laparēn tetato mega te stibaron te,
oimēsen de aleis hōs t’ aietos hypsipetēeis,
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, he drew his sharp sword,
which hung beneath his flank, great and stout,
and he swooped, gathering himself, like an eagle high-flying,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and drew his sharp sword, which hung beneath his flank, great and stout, and gathering himself he swooped down like a high-flying eagle,
sentences.n: A new paragraph: Hector acts. εἰρύσσατο is the aorist of ἐρύω ‘draw’ (the middle voice: he draws it for himself), and the sword hung ὑπὸ λαπάρην ‘under the flank’; τέτατο is the pluperfect passive of τείνω, ‘was stretched, hung’. Line 308 is a line the Odyssey also has, in the same words (24.538, the eagle simile), and its English is reused: ἀλεὶς is the aorist passive participle of εἴλω ‘press together’, ‘gathering himself’, and ὑψιπετήεις ‘high-flying’ is a fixed epithet of the eagle. The comparison runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὅς τ’ εἶσιν πεδίον δὲ διὰ νεφέων ἐρεβεννῶν
ἁρπάξων ἢ ἄρν’ ἀμαλὴν ἤ πτῶκα λαγωόν·
ὣς Ἕκτωρ οἴμησε τινάσσων φάσγανον ὀξύ.
sentences.tr:
hos t’ eisin pedion de dia nepheōn erebennōn
harpaxōn ē arn’ amalēn ē ptōka lagōon·
hōs Hektōr oimēse tinassōn phasganon oxy.
sentences.i: that goes to the plain through the murky clouds to snatch a tender lamb or a cowering hare; so Hector swooped, swinging his sharp sword.
sentences.n: The simile concludes. ὅς τ’ εἶσιν is a relative clause, ‘which goes’, with the general-statement τε; εἶσιν is the present of εἶμι ‘go’; πεδίον δέ is πεδίον plus the ending -δε, ‘to the plain’. ἐρεβεννῶν ‘murky’ describes the clouds. ἁρπάξων is the future participle of ἁρπάζω in its sense of purpose, ‘to snatch’. πτῶκα means ‘cowering one’, from a verb for crouching in fear, and λαγωόν is ‘hare’. Line 311 returns from the picture: ὣς … οἴμησε ‘so he swooped’, with τινάσσων ‘swinging’ the sword.

sentences.t:
ὁρμήθη δ’ Ἀχιλεύς, μένεος δ’ ἐμπλήσατο θυμὸν
ἀγρίου, πρόσθεν δὲ σάκος στέρνοιο κάλυψε
καλὸν δαιδάλεον, κόρυθι δ’ ἐπένευε φαεινῇ
τετραφάλῳ·
sentences.tr:
hormēthē d’ Achileus, meneos d’ emplēsato thymon
agriou, prosthen de sakos sternoio kalypse
kalon daidaleon, korythi d’ epeneue phaeinēi
tetraphalōi·
sentences.l:
And Achilles rushed, and filled his heart with savage
might, and in front the shield covered his chest,
fair, cunningly wrought, and with his shining helmet he nodded,
four-ridged;
sentences.i: Achilles charged, and filled his heart with savage might; in front of him the fair, cunningly wrought shield covered his chest, and he nodded with his shining four-ridged helmet;
sentences.n: Achilles is shown in full arms, the armour Hephaestus made. ὁρμήθη is the aorist passive of ὁρμάω ‘rush’, and μένεος ἐμπλήσατο θυμὸν ἀγρίου is ‘filled his heart with savage might’, with μένεος the genitive of what fills it. In πρόσθεν δὲ σάκος στέρνοιο κάλυψε the shield (σάκος) is the subject and the chest (στέρνοιο, genitive) what it covers. δαιδάλεον is ‘cunningly wrought’; κόρυθι … φαεινῇ τετραφάλῳ is the dative of κόρυς ‘helmet’ with ‘shining’ and ‘four-ridged’ (the sense of τετράφαλος is uncertain), and ἐπένευε is ‘nodded’, the crest moving with it. The unit ends at the stop in the middle of line 315. Line 314 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the opening syllable of καλόν, short by nature, has to count long, and so has the last syllable of κόρυθι in the fourth foot.

sentences.t:
καλαὶ δὲ περισσείοντο ἔθειραι
χρύσεαι, ἃς Ἥφαιστος ἵει λόφον ἀμφὶ θαμειάς.
sentences.tr:
kalai de perisseionto etheirai
chryseai, has Hēphaistos hiei lophon amphi thameias.
sentences.l:
and fair plumes were shaken about,
golden, which Hephaestus set around the crest, thick ones.
sentences.i: and the fair golden plumes shook all about it, which Hephaestus had set thickly around the crest.
sentences.n: The plumes of the helmet. περισσείοντο is the imperfect passive of περισσείω ‘shake about’, so the plumes (ἔθειραι, the ‘hair’ of the crest) are the subject, καλαί ‘fair’ and χρύσεαι ‘golden’ their adjectives. ἵει is the unaugmented imperfect of ἵημι, here ‘set’, and θαμειάς ‘thick’ goes with the plumes. Line 316 stands in the same words at 19.383, and the English shipped there is reused.

sentences.t:
οἷος δ’ ἀστὴρ εἶσι μετ’ ἀστράσι νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ
ἕσπερος, ὃς κάλλιστος ἐν οὐρανῷ ἵσταται ἀστήρ,
sentences.tr:
hoios d’ astēr eisi met’ astrasi nyktos amolgōi
hesperos, hos kallistos en ouranōi histatai astēr,
sentences.l:
And as a star goes among the stars in the dead of night,
the evening star, which is the fairest star standing in heaven,
sentences.i: And as the star goes among the stars in the depths of the night, the evening star, the fairest star that stands in the sky,
sentences.n: A simile for the gleam of the spear-point, completed in the next unit. οἷος ‘such as’ opens it and ἕσπερος names the evening star, Hesperus; ἵσταται ‘stands’ is the present middle of ἵστημι. The sense of ἀμολγῷ in νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ is not known (the ancients guessed ‘milking-time’ or ‘darkness’); we read the phrase as ‘in the depths of the night’, as elsewhere. κάλλιστος is the superlative of καλός.

sentences.t:
ὣς αἰχμῆς ἀπέλαμπ’ εὐήκεος, ἣν ἄρ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
πάλλεν δεξιτερῇ φρονέων κακὸν Ἕκτορι δίῳ,
εἰσορόων χρόα καλόν, ὅπῃ εἴξειε μάλιστα.
sentences.tr:
hōs aichmēs apelamp’ euēkeos, hēn ar’ Achilleus
pallen dexiterēi phroneōn kakon Hektori diōi,
eisoroōn chroa kalon, hopēi eixeie malista.
sentences.l:
so shone from the well-pointed spear-point, which Achilles
was shaking in his right hand, devising evil for heavenly Hector,
looking at his fair skin, where it would give way most.
sentences.i: So the light shone from the well-pointed spear-point that Achilles shook in his right hand, with evil in his mind for heavenly Hector, as he eyed his fair skin to see where it would give way most easily.
sentences.n: ὣς … ἀπέλαμπ’ completes the comparison with the star: the point (αἰχμῆς, genitive) gave off light like it. εὐήκεος ‘well-pointed’ goes with it. ἥν is the relative, ‘which’, with ἄρα, and πάλλεν is the unaugmented imperfect of πάλλω ‘shake’; φρονέων κακόν ‘thinking evil’ is said of Achilles’ purpose. εἰσορόων is the participle of εἰσοράω ‘look at’ and χρόα καλόν is ‘fair skin’, as at 5.858. ὅπῃ εἴξειε μάλιστα is an indirect question in the optative, ‘where it would yield most’, and the subject is the skin.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δὲ καὶ ἄλλο τόσον μὲν ἔχε χρόα χάλκεα τεύχεα,
καλά, τὰ Πατρόκλοιο βίην ἐνάριξε κατακτάς·
sentences.tr:
tou de kai allo toson men eche chroa chalkea teuchea,
kala, ta Patrokloio biēn enarixe kataktas·
sentences.l:
And of him, the rest, so much of the skin, the bronze armour held,
fine armour, which he stripped from the might of Patroclus, having killed him;
sentences.i: The rest of his skin, as far as it went, the bronze armour covered, the fine armour he had stripped from the might of Patroclus when he killed him;
sentences.n: Hector wears the armour of Achilles that Patroclus had borrowed. The text is hard: τοῦ δὲ καὶ ἄλλο τόσον … ἔχε χρόα χάλκεα τεύχεα reads ‘and the rest of his skin, as much of it, the bronze armour held (covered)’, with ἔχε the unaugmented imperfect, and τόσον a quantity ‘so much’. τεύχεα is ‘armour’ and καλά ‘fine’. Πατρόκλοιο βίην is the periphrasis ‘the might of Patroclus’ for Patroclus himself, and ἐνάριξε is the aorist of ἐναρίζω ‘strip of arms’; κατακτάς is ‘having killed’, an aorist participle of κατακτείνω.

sentences.t:
φαίνετο δ’ ᾗ κληῗδες ἀπ’ ὤμων αὐχέν’ ἔχουσι,
λαυκανίην, ἵνα τε ψυχῆς ὤκιστος ὄλεθρος·
sentences.tr:
phaineto d’ hēi klēïdes ap’ ōmōn auchen’ echousi,
laukaniēn, hina te psychēs ōkistos olethros·
sentences.l:
and there showed, where the collar-bones hold the neck apart from the shoulders,
the throat, where the destruction of life is swiftest;
sentences.i: but one place showed, where the collar-bones hold the neck apart from the shoulders, the throat, where the destruction of life comes swiftest;
sentences.n: The one gap in the armour, between the collar-bones. φαίνετο is ‘it showed, was visible’, with no subject stated in the Greek. κληῗδες is the nominative plural of κλείς ‘collar-bone’, with the diaeresis printed, and ἀπ’ ὤμων αὐχέν’ ἔχουσι is ‘keep the neck apart from the shoulders’. λαυκανίην ‘throat’ is in apposition to αὐχέν’, the neck the collar-bones hold apart, and the English supplies ‘one place’ for the subject of φαίνετο. ἵνα τε is ‘where’; ψυχῆς ὄλεθρος is ‘the destruction of the life’, and ὤκιστος is the superlative of ὠκύς ‘swift’.

sentences.t:
τῇ ῥ’ ἐπὶ οἷ μεμαῶτ’ ἔλασ’ ἔγχεϊ δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
ἀντικρὺ δ’ ἁπαλοῖο δι’ αὐχένος ἤλυθ’ ἀκωκή·
sentences.tr:
tēi rh’ epi hoi memaōt’ elas’ encheï dios Achilleus,
antikry d’ hapaloio di’ auchenos ēlyth’ akōkē·
sentences.l:
There at him, as he charged, drove with his spear heavenly Achilles,
and straight through the tender neck went the point;
sentences.i: Heavenly Achilles drove his spear at that spot as Hector charged at him, and the point went straight through his tender neck;
sentences.n: The blow. τῇ is ‘there, at that spot’, ἔλασ’ the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’ with the elision of its final vowel, and μεμαῶτ’ the perfect participle of μέμαα ‘be eager’, ‘as he (Hector) charged’, agreeing with an understood him. Line 327 stands in the same words at 17.49, and the English shipped there is reused: ἀντικρύ ‘straight through’, ἁπαλοῖο ‘tender’, ἀκωκή ‘point’. ἤλυθ’ is the aorist of ἔρχομαι.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἀπ’ ἀσφάραγον μελίη τάμε χαλκοβάρεια,
ὄφρά τί μιν προτιείποι ἀμειβόμενος ἐπέεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ ap’ aspharagon meliē tame chalkobareia,
ophra ti min protieipoi ameibomenos epeessin.
sentences.l:
and the ash-spear, bronze-heavy, did not cut through the windpipe,
so that he might still say something to him in answer.
sentences.i: and the bronze-weighted ash spear did not sever the windpipe, so that Hector could still answer him and say something to him.
sentences.n: Hector can still speak. μελίη (‘ash’) is the spear, made of ash-wood, and χαλκοβάρεια ‘bronze-heavy’ is a rare epithet formed from χαλκός and βαρύς. ἀπ’ … τάμε is ‘cut off, severed’, a verb split from its preposition (tmesis), with ἀσφάραγον the windpipe. ὄφρα with the optative προτιείποι gives purpose, ‘so that he might say’, and ἀμειβόμενος ἐπέεσσιν is ‘answering with words’.

sentences.t: ἤριπε δ’ ἐν κονίῃς· ὃ δ’ ἐπεύξατο δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ēripe d’ en koniēis· ho d’ epeuxato dios Achilleus·
sentences.l: And he crashed down in the dust; and he vaunted over him, heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: Hector crashed down in the dust, and heavenly Achilles cried out in triumph over him:
sentences.n: ἤριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω, ‘crashed down’, with the plural κονίῃς ‘dust’ for a single fall. ὃ δ’ ἐπεύξατο is the speech introduction of one who gloats: ἐπεύχομαι is ‘vaunt, cry out in triumph’, and ὃ δ’ is Achilles, named in the same line.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἀτάρ που ἔφης Πατροκλῆ’ ἐξεναρίζων
σῶς ἔσσεσθ’, ἐμὲ δ’ οὐδὲν ὀπίζεο νόσφιν ἐόντα,
sentences.tr:
Hektor atar pou ephēs Patroklē’ exenarizōn
sōs essesth’, eme d’ ouden opizeo nosphin eonta,
sentences.l:
“Hector, but you said, I suppose, while despoiling Patroclus,
that you would be safe, and you in no way respected me, being apart,
sentences.i: “Hector, you said, I suppose, as you were stripping Patroclus of his armour, that you would be safe, and you had no respect for me, since I was far away,
sentences.n: Achilles’ answer is a taunt. ἀτάρ που is ‘but I suppose’, mocking; ἔφης is ‘you said’ (or thought). ἐξεναρίζων is the present participle of ἐξεναρίζω ‘strip of armour’, and σῶς ἔσσεσθ’ is ‘that you would be safe’, with ἔσσεσθαι the epic future infinitive. ἐμὲ δ’ οὐδὲν ὀπίζεο ‘you in no way feared me’ has ὀπίζεο the imperfect middle of ὀπίζομαι, and νόσφιν ἐόντα ‘being apart’ agrees with ἐμέ.

sentences.t:
νήπιε· τοῖο δ’ ἄνευθεν ἀοσσητὴρ μέγ’ ἀμείνων
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ἐγὼ μετόπισθε λελείμμην,
ὅς τοι γούνατ’ ἔλυσα·
sentences.tr:
nēpie· toio d’ aneuthen aossētēr meg’ ameinōn
nēusin epi glaphyrēisin egō metopisthe leleimmēn,
hos toi gounat’ elysa·
sentences.i: foolish one; but apart from him a far better helper was left behind by the hollow ships, I, who have loosened your knees;
sentences.n: ‘He’ (τοῖο) is Patroclus; Achilles is the better helper (ἀοσσητήρ) who stayed behind. νήπιε ‘foolish one’ is a vocative that is a rebuke. λελείμμην is the pluperfect passive of λείπω, ‘I had been left behind’. ὅς τοι γούνατ’ ἔλυσα has a relative ὅς in the third person after ἐγώ in the first, so ‘I, who’, and ‘to loosen the knees’ is to kill. The unit ends at the stop in the middle of line 335.

sentences.t:
σὲ μὲν κύνες ἠδ’ οἰωνοὶ
ἑλκήσουσ’ ἀϊκῶς, τὸν δὲ κτεριοῦσιν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
se men kynes ēd’ oiōnoi
helkēsous’ aïkōs, ton de kteriousin Achaioi.
sentences.l:
you the dogs and the birds
will drag about in unseemly fashion, but to him the Achaeans will render funeral rites.”
sentences.i: the dogs and the birds will drag you about in unseemly fashion, but the Achaeans will pay him funeral honours.”
sentences.n: σὲ μὲν … τὸν δέ sets Hector and Patroclus against each other, ‘you … but him’. ἑλκήσουσι is the future of ἑλκέω, the by-form of ἕλκω ‘drag’, and ἀϊκῶς is an adverb which seems to belong with ἀεικής ‘unseemly’. κτεριοῦσιν is the future of κτερίζω ‘render funeral rites’, with κτέρεα the gifts and honours due to the dead. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ὀλιγοδρανέων προσέφη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ oligodraneōn prosephē korythaiolos Hektōr·
sentences.l: Him, weak, addressed Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Weak as he was, Hector of the glancing helmet said to him:
sentences.n: A whole-line reply formula, in the same words at 15.246, whose English is reused. ὀλιγοδρανέων ‘weak’ (literally ‘having little strength’) is the participle, and κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is Hector’s fixed epithet. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘address’. Hector is now dying.

sentences.t:
λίσσομ’ ὑπὲρ ψυχῆς καὶ γούνων σῶν τε τοκήων,
μή με ἔα παρὰ νηυσὶ κύνας καταδάψαι Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.tr:
lissom’ hyper psychēs kai gounōn sōn te tokēōn,
mē me ea para nēusi kynas katadapsai Achaiōn,
sentences.l:
“I beg you by your life and your knees and your parents,
do not let the dogs devour me beside the ships of the Achaeans,
sentences.i: “I beg you by your life, by your knees and by your parents: do not let the dogs devour me beside the ships of the Achaeans,
sentences.n: λίσσομαι ‘I beg’ takes ὑπέρ with the genitive for the thing begged by: ψυχῆς ‘your life’, γούνων ‘knees’ (a suppliant touches the knees), τοκήων ‘parents’ (the epic form of τοκέων). μή με ἔα is ‘do not let me’, with ἔα the imperative of ἐάω, and καταδάψαι is the aorist infinitive of καταδάπτω ‘tear, devour’, κύνας the accusative of its subject.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν χαλκόν τε ἅλις χρυσόν τε δέδεξο,
δῶρα τά τοι δώσουσι πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ,
sentences.tr:
alla sy men chalkon te halis chryson te dedexo,
dōra ta toi dōsousi patēr kai potnia mētēr,
sentences.l:
but you, accept bronze in plenty and gold,
gifts that my father and my lady mother will give you,
sentences.i: but accept bronze and gold in plenty, the gifts that my father and my lady mother will give you,
sentences.n: Hector offers ransom. δέδεξο is the perfect imperative of δέχομαι ‘accept’ and ἅλις means ‘in plenty’. δῶρα τά τοι δώσουσι: τά is the relative ‘which’, τοι is σοι ‘to you’, and the subjects are πατήρ (Priam) and πότνια μήτηρ (Hecuba). πότνια ‘lady’ is the house word for it.

sentences.t:
σῶμα δὲ οἴκαδ’ ἐμὸν δόμεναι πάλιν, ὄφρα πυρός με
Τρῶες καὶ Τρώων ἄλοχοι λελάχωσι θανόντα.
sentences.tr:
sōma de oikad’ emon domenai palin, ophra pyros me
Trōes kai Trōōn alochoi lelachōsi thanonta.
sentences.l:
but my body home to give back, so that of fire me
the Trojans and the wives of the Trojans may give a share, when I am dead.”
sentences.i: and give my body back home, so that the Trojans and the Trojans’ wives may give me my share of fire when I am dead.”
sentences.n: δόμεναι is an infinitive used as an imperative, ‘give back’, and σῶμα δὲ οἴκαδ’ ἐμὸν … πάλιν ‘my body, home again’. The two lines stand in the same words at 7.79–80; the English there is reused, with the sentence frame changed to fit what comes before. λελάχωσι is the aorist subjunctive of λαγχάνω ‘obtain a share’ with πυρός ‘of fire’ (the funeral pyre), and θανόντα ‘when I am dead’ agrees with με. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεὺς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Then Achilles, swift of foot, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: A reply formula, with the same first half as the Odyssey’s τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη. ὑπόδρα means ‘with a scowl’, though its exact origin is not certain, and ἰδών is the aorist participle of ὁράω. πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’ is Achilles’ fixed epithet, with πόδας an accusative of respect.

sentences.t: μή με κύον γούνων γουνάζεο μὴ δὲ τοκήων·
sentences.tr: mē me kyon gounōn gounazeo mē de tokēōn·
sentences.l: “Do not, dog, entreat me by my knees nor by my parents;
sentences.i: “Do not entreat me by my knees or my parents, dog;
sentences.n: Achilles turns Hector’s words back. κύον is the vocative of κύων ‘dog’, an insult, and γουνάζεο is the imperative middle of γουνάζομαι ‘entreat’, with γούνων ‘by (the) knees’ and τοκήων ‘by (the) parents’ in the genitive. μή … μὴ δέ is ‘do not … and not’.

sentences.t:
αἲ γάρ πως αὐτόν με μένος καὶ θυμὸς ἀνήη
ὤμ’ ἀποταμνόμενον κρέα ἔδμεναι, οἷα ἔοργας,
ὡς οὐκ ἔσθ’ ὃς σῆς γε κύνας κεφαλῆς ἀπαλάλκοι,
sentences.tr:
ai gar pōs auton me menos kai thymos anēē
ōm’ apotamnomenon krea edmenai, hoia eorgas,
hōs ouk esth’ hos sēs ge kynas kephalēs apalalkoi,
sentences.l:
would that my might and my heart would somehow urge me myself
to cut off your flesh and eat it raw, for what you have done,
so surely is there no one who could keep the dogs from your head,
sentences.i: If only my might and my heart would somehow drive me to cut off your flesh and eat it raw, myself, for what you have done! As surely as there is no one who can keep the dogs from your head,
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ introduces a wish, ‘would that’, with the optative ἀνήη (‘drive, urge on’, from ἀνίημι), and its subject is μένος καὶ θυμός ‘might and heart’; με is the object. ὤμ’ is ὠμά ‘raw’, with κρέα ‘flesh’. ἀποταμνόμενον is ‘cutting off (for myself)’ and ἔδμεναι the epic infinitive ‘to eat’. οἷα ἔοργας is ‘for such things as you have done’, with ἔοργας the perfect of ῥέζω. ὡς οὐκ ἔσθ’ ὅς is ‘as surely as there is no one who’: ἀπαλάλκοι is an optative of ἀπαλέξω, ‘keep off’. The sentence runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εἴ κεν δεκάκις τε καὶ εἰκοσινήριτ’ ἄποινα
στήσωσ’ ἐνθάδ’ ἄγοντες, ὑπόσχωνται δὲ καὶ ἄλλα,
οὐδ’ εἴ κέν σ’ αὐτὸν χρυσῷ ἐρύσασθαι ἀνώγοι
Δαρδανίδης Πρίαμος·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ei ken dekakis te kai eikosinērit’ apoina
stēsōs’ enthad’ agontes, hyposchōntai de kai alla,
oud’ ei ken s’ auton chrysōi erysasthai anōgoi
Dardanidēs Priamos·
sentences.l:
not even if ten times and twenty times over a ransom
they should set down here, bringing it, and promise other things besides,
not even if he should bid them redeem you yourself with gold,
Priam, Dardanus’ descendant;
sentences.i: not even if they should set down here, bringing it, ten and twenty times as much ransom, and promise still more, not even if Priam, a descendant of Dardanus, should bid them buy you back with gold;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ εἴ κεν … οὐδ’ εἴ κέν … is ‘not even if … not even if’. εἰκοσινήριτα is a rare word, apparently ‘twenty-fold’, and δεκάκις ‘ten times’; the sense of the second part is not known. ἄποινα is ‘ransom’, and στήσωσ’ is the aorist subjunctive of ἵστημι, ‘set (it) down’, perhaps in the scale. ὑπόσχωνται ‘promise’ is the middle aorist subjunctive. ἐρύσασθαι ‘to redeem’ (to draw someone back out of danger) has the gold, χρυσῷ, as the price. Δαρδανίδης is a patronymic from the ancestor, ‘descendant of Dardanus’, here Priam. The unit ends at the stop in the middle of line 352.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὧς σέ γε πότνια μήτηρ
ἐνθεμένη λεχέεσσι γοήσεται ὃν τέκεν αὐτή,
ἀλλὰ κύνες τε καὶ οἰωνοὶ κατὰ πάντα δάσονται.
sentences.tr:
oud’ hōs se ge potnia mētēr
enthemenē lecheessi goēsetai hon teken autē,
alla kynes te kai oiōnoi kata panta dasontai.
sentences.l:
not even so will your lady mother,
having laid you on the bier, lament you whom she herself bore,
but the dogs and the birds will share you out in every part.”
sentences.i: not even so will your lady mother lay you on the bier and lament you, whom she herself bore; the dogs and the birds will divide you up, every part of you.”
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὧς is ‘not even so’, ὧς being the old adverb ‘thus’. ἐνθεμένη is the aorist middle participle of ἐντίθημι, ‘having laid (you)’, with λεχέεσσι the epic dative plural of λέχος ‘bed’, here the bier. γοήσεται is the future middle of γοάω ‘lament’, and ὃν τέκεν αὐτή is ‘whom she herself bore’, with ὅν the relative. δάσονται is the future middle of δαίομαι ‘divide, share out’, and κατὰ πάντα ‘in every part’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ καταθνῄσκων προσέφη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: ton de katathnēiskōn prosephē korythaiolos Hektōr·
sentences.l: Him, dying, addressed Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Dying, Hector of the glancing helmet said to him:
sentences.n: Hector’s last speech is introduced like his first. καταθνῄσκων ‘dying’ is the present participle of καταθνῄσκω; the present stresses that he is in the act of dying.

sentences.t:
ἦ σ’ εὖ γιγνώσκων προτιόσσομαι, οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλον
πείσειν· ἦ γὰρ σοί γε σιδήρεος ἐν φρεσὶ θυμός.
sentences.tr:
ē s’ eu gignōskōn protiossomai, oud’ ar’ emellon
peisein· ē gar soi ge sidēreos en phresi thymos.
sentences.l:
“Truly I look at you and know you well, and I was not going
to persuade you; for truly the heart in your wits is of iron.
sentences.i: “Truly I know you well as I look at you, and I was never going to persuade you; for the heart in your mind is iron.
sentences.n: ἦ σ’ εὖ γιγνώσκων προτιόσσομαι is ‘truly, knowing you well, I look at you’, and the verb προτιόσσομαι means ‘look at’ or ‘foresee’. οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλον πείσειν: μέλλω with the future infinitive is ‘be going to’, so ‘I was not going to persuade’. σιδήρεος ‘of iron’ is a predicate to θυμός, and ἐν φρεσί ‘in your wits’ is a locative.

sentences.t:
φράζεο νῦν, μή τοί τι θεῶν μήνιμα γένωμαι
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε κέν σε Πάρις καὶ Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
ἐσθλὸν ἐόντ’ ὀλέσωσιν ἐνὶ Σκαιῇσι πύλῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
phrazeo nyn, mē toi ti theōn mēnima genōmai
ēmati tōi hote ken se Paris kai Phoibos Apollōn
esthlon eont’ olesōsin eni Skaiēisi pylēisin.
sentences.l:
Take care now, lest I become for you some cause of the gods’ wrath
on the day when Paris and Phoebus Apollo shall destroy you,
good as you are, at the Scaean Gates.”
sentences.i: Take care now that I do not become a cause of the gods’ wrath against you on the day when Paris and Phoebus Apollo destroy you, good warrior that you are, at the Scaean Gates.”
sentences.n: The dying Hector foretells Achilles’ own death. φράζεο is the imperative middle ‘take care’, and μή τοι … γένωμαι ‘lest I become to you’ is a clause of fear, with the aorist subjunctive and τοι = σοι. θεῶν μήνιμα is ‘something that raises the gods’ wrath’. ἤματι τῷ ὅτε κεν … ὀλέσωσιν is ‘on the day when they shall destroy’ with aorist subjunctive. ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα ‘being good’ agrees with σέ; ἐσθλός of a man in battle is the house ‘good’, meaning one who is brave in the fight. Σκαιῇσι πύλῃσιν is the dative plural of the Scaean Gates. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα μιν εἰπόντα τέλος θανάτοιο κάλυψε,
sentences.tr: hōs ara min eiponta telos thanatoio kalypse,
sentences.l: So then, as he spoke, the end of death covered him;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the end that death brings covered him;
sentences.n: The line stands in the same words at 16.855, and its English is reused. εἰπόντα ‘as he spoke’ is the aorist participle of εἶπον, and τέλος θανάτοιο is ‘the end of death’, ‘the end that death brings’. κάλυψε is the aorist of καλύπτω ‘cover’.

sentences.t:
ψυχὴ δ’ ἐκ ῥεθέων πταμένη Ἄϊδος δὲ βεβήκει
ὃν πότμον γοόωσα λιποῦσ’ ἀνδροτῆτα καὶ ἥβην.
sentences.tr:
psychē d’ ek rhetheōn ptamenē Aïdos de bebēkei
hon potmon gooōsa lipous’ androtēta kai hēbēn.
sentences.l:
and the soul out of his limbs, having flown, to Hades went,
bewailing its doom, leaving manhood and youth.
sentences.i: and his soul flew from his limbs and went to the house of Hades, wailing its doom, leaving manhood and youth.
sentences.n: The two lines stand in the same words at 16.856–857, and their shipped English is reused. ψυχή is the ‘soul’ that survives the body; ῥεθέων is the epic genitive plural ‘limbs’, and πταμένη the participle of a verb ‘fly’. Ἄϊδος δέ has the ending -δε, ‘to Hades’, with ‘house’ understood. βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, and ὃν πότμον γοόωσα is ‘bewailing its doom’, ὅν being possessive. Line 363 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of ἀνδροτῆτα is closed and so long by position, but the metre needs it short.

sentences.t: τὸν καὶ τεθνηῶτα προσηύδα δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton kai tethnēōta prosēuda dios Achilleus·
sentences.l: To him, even dead, spoke heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: Heavenly Achilles spoke to him even in death:
sentences.n: τεθνηῶτα is the perfect participle of θνῄσκω, ‘having died, dead’, agreeing with τόν. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’, and καί is ‘even’.

sentences.t:
τέθναθι· κῆρα δ’ ἐγὼ τότε δέξομαι ὁππότε κεν δὴ
Ζεὺς ἐθέλῃ τελέσαι ἠδ’ ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.tr:
tethnathi· kēra d’ egō tote dexomai hoppote ken dē
Zeus ethelēi telesai ēd’ athanatoi theoi alloi.
sentences.l:
“Die; and the death-fate I will then accept, whenever
Zeus wishes to bring it about, and the other immortal gods.”
sentences.i: “Die; and I shall accept my fated death whenever Zeus wishes to bring it about, and the other immortal gods.”
sentences.n: τέθναθι is the perfect imperative of θνῄσκω, ‘be dead’, a harsh way to say ‘die’. Line 366 and the second half of 365 stand in the same words at 18.115–116, and the English shipped there is reused. κῆρα is the accusative of κήρ ‘death-fate’ (not κῆρ ‘heart’). ὁππότε κεν … ἐθέλῃ is a subjunctive, ‘whenever (Zeus) shall wish’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἐκ νεκροῖο ἐρύσσατο χάλκεον ἔγχος,
καὶ τό γ’ ἄνευθεν ἔθηχ’, ὃ δ’ ἀπ’ ὤμων τεύχε’ ἐσύλα
αἱματόεντ’·
sentences.tr:
ē rha, kai ek nekroio eryssato chalkeon enchos,
kai to g’ aneuthen ethēch’, ho d’ ap’ ōmōn teuche’ esyla
haimatoent’·
sentences.i: So he said, and drew his bronze spear out of the corpse and laid it aside, and began to strip the blood-stained armour from the shoulders;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ἐρύσσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρύω ‘draw out’, and ἔθηχ’ is ἔθηκε (with χ for κ before the rough breathing of ὃ), ‘laid, put’; ἄνευθεν ‘aside’. The imperfect ἐσύλα (‘was stripping’) starts the action that continues in the next unit. τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’, and αἱματόεντ’ ‘blood-stained’ agrees with it, placed in the next line. The unit ends at the stop in the middle of line 369.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοι δὲ περίδραμον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν,
οἳ καὶ θηήσαντο φυὴν καὶ εἶδος ἀγητὸν
Ἕκτορος· οὐδ’ ἄρα οἵ τις ἀνουτητί γε παρέστη.
sentences.tr:
alloi de peridramon huies Achaiōn,
hoi kai thēēsanto phyēn kai eidos agēton
Hektoros· oud’ ara hoi tis anoutēti ge parestē.
sentences.l:
and the others ran around, the sons of the Achaeans,
who wondered at the stature and the admirable form
of Hector; and no one stood by him without wounding him.
sentences.i: and the other sons of the Achaeans ran up around him, and they marvelled at Hector’s stature and his admirable form; and not one stood beside him without wounding him.
sentences.n: ἄλλοι … υἷες Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the other sons of the Achaeans’, ‘sons of the Achaeans’ being a fixed phrase. περίδραμον is the aorist of περιτρέχω ‘run around’, and θηήσαντο is the aorist middle of θηέομαι ‘gaze at’. φυήν is ‘stature’ and εἶδος ἀγητόν ‘admirable form’. ἀνουτητί (‘without a wound’) is formed from οὐτάω ‘wound’ with the negative ἀ-; οὐδ’ ἄρα … τις is ‘and not one’, and οἵ, the dative οἱ ‘him’ accented before the enclitic τις, goes with παρέστη ‘stood beside him’ (aorist of παρίστημι).

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν ἰδὼν ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον·
sentences.tr: hōde de tis eipesken idōn es plēsion allon·
sentences.l: And thus someone would say, looking to another close by:
sentences.i: And as each looked at the one beside him, he would say something like this:
sentences.n: The line stands in the same words at 2.271, and its English is reused. εἴπεσκεν is an iterative imperfect, formed with -σκ-, that means ‘would say (again and again)’. τις is ‘someone’, and ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον is ‘to another close by’. A bystander’s speech follows.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ἦ μάλα δὴ μαλακώτερος ἀμφαφάασθαι
Ἕκτωρ ἢ ὅτε νῆας ἐνέπρησεν πυρὶ κηλέῳ.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi, ē mala dē malakōteros amphaphaasthai
Hektōr ē hote nēas eneprēsen pyri kēleōi.
sentences.l:
“Ah, truly now softer to handle
is Hector than when he set the ships on fire with blazing fire.”
sentences.i: “Ah, Hector is truly much softer to handle now than when he burned the ships with blazing fire.”
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is a cry of surprise, ‘Ah!’. μαλακώτερος is the comparative of μαλακός ‘soft’, and ἀμφαφάασθαι is an infinitive of respect, ‘to handle, to touch’. ἢ ὅτε is ‘than when’. ἐνέπρησεν is the aorist of ἐμπίπρημι ‘set on fire’, and πυρὶ κηλέῳ is ‘with blazing fire’. The fire is the one Hector brought to the Achaean ships earlier in the poem. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα τις εἴπεσκε καὶ οὐτήσασκε παραστάς.
sentences.tr: hōs ara tis eipeske kai outēsaske parastas.
sentences.l: So then each would say, and would wound him, standing beside him.
sentences.i: So each would speak, and standing beside him would wound him.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. εἴπεσκε and οὐτήσασκε are iterative past tenses (formed with -σκ-), ‘would say’ and ‘would wound’, repeated by many men. τις is ‘each’, and παραστάς is the aorist participle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐπεὶ ἐξενάριξε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
στὰς ἐν Ἀχαιοῖσιν ἔπεα πτερόεντ’ ἀγόρευεν·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ epei exenarixe podarkēs dios Achilleus,
stas en Achaioisin epea pteroent’ agoreuen·
sentences.l:
And when he had despoiled him, swift-footed, heavenly Achilles,
standing among the Achaeans he spoke winged words:
sentences.i: And when swift-footed, heavenly Achilles had stripped him of his armour, he stood among the Achaeans and spoke winged words:
sentences.n: ἐξενάριξε is ‘despoiled’ (killed and stripped, here only stripped, since Hector is already dead). ποδάρκης ‘swift-footed’ is a fixed epithet of Achilles. στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the stock phrase, here with ἀγόρευεν ‘spoke (in assembly)’.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
ἐπεὶ δὴ τόνδ’ ἄνδρα θεοὶ δαμάσασθαι ἔδωκαν,
ὃς κακὰ πόλλ’ ἔρρεξεν ὅσ’ οὐ σύμπαντες οἱ ἄλλοι,
sentences.tr:
ō philoi Argeiōn hēgētores ēde medontes
epei dē tond’ andra theoi damasasthai edōkan,
hos kaka poll’ errexen hos’ ou sympantes hoi alloi,
sentences.l:
“O friends, leaders and lords of the Argives,
since the gods have granted us to subdue this man,
who did much evil, as much as not all the others together,
sentences.i: “Friends, leaders and lords of the Argives: since the gods have granted that this man be overcome, who did more evil than all the others together,
sentences.n: Achilles calls the chiefs of the army together. ὦ φίλοι … ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες is the address of 2.79, whose English is reused for it. ἐπεὶ δή is ‘since’, with τόνδε ἄνδρα ‘this man’; δαμάσασθαι is the aorist infinitive of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, and ἔδωκαν the aorist ‘granted’. ὅσ’ οὐ σύμπαντες οἱ ἄλλοι is ‘as many as all the others together did not’, which means more than all the rest did. In line 379 the opening syllable of ἐπεί, short by nature, has to count long.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄγετ’ ἀμφὶ πόλιν σὺν τεύχεσι πειρηθῶμεν,
ὄφρά κ’ ἔτι γνῶμεν Τρώων νόον ὅν τιν’ ἔχουσιν,
ἢ καταλείψουσιν πόλιν ἄκρην τοῦδε πεσόντος,
ἦε μένειν μεμάασι καὶ Ἕκτορος οὐκέτ’ ἐόντος.
sentences.tr:
ei d’ aget’ amphi polin syn teuchesi peirēthōmen,
ophra k’ eti gnōmen Trōōn noon hon tin’ echousin,
ē kataleipsousin polin akrēn toude pesontos,
ēe menein memaasi kai Hektoros ouket’ eontos.
sentences.l:
come, let us make a trial round the city with our armour,
that we may learn still what mind the Trojans have,
whether they will leave the high city now this man has fallen,
or are eager to stay, though Hector is no more.
sentences.i: come, let us test them in arms around the city, so that we may learn what the Trojans have in mind: whether they will abandon the city on its height now that this man has fallen, or are eager to stay although Hector is no more.
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἄγετε is an urgent ‘come now’, followed by πειρηθῶμεν ‘let us make a trial’, the aorist subjunctive. ὄφρα κε γνῶμεν is ‘so that we may learn’, and Τρώων νόον ὅν τιν’ ἔχουσιν is ‘what mind the Trojans have’. The question runs ἢ καταλείψουσιν … ἦε μένειν μεμάασι, ‘whether they will leave … or are eager to stay’; μεμάασι is the perfect of μέμαα. πόλιν ἄκρην is the high city (the citadel on the heights); τοῦδε πεσόντος and Ἕκτορος οὐκέτ’ ἐόντος are genitives absolute, ‘this man having fallen’ and ‘Hector being no more’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τί ἤ μοι ταῦτα φίλος διελέξατο θυμός;
sentences.tr: alla ti ē moi tauta philos dielexato thymos;
sentences.l: But why indeed has my dear heart talked these things over with me?
sentences.i: But why has my own heart talked all this over with me?
sentences.n: Achilles checks himself. The line stands in the same words at 11.407, and its English is reused. ἀλλὰ τί ἤ is ‘but why indeed’, and διελέξατο is the aorist middle of διαλέγομαι, ‘talked over’; the question is rhetorical, and the thought of the city is dropped.

sentences.t:
κεῖται πὰρ νήεσσι νέκυς ἄκλαυτος ἄθαπτος
Πάτροκλος· τοῦ δ’ οὐκ ἐπιλήσομαι, ὄφρ’ ἂν ἔγωγε
ζωοῖσιν μετέω καί μοι φίλα γούνατ’ ὀρώρῃ·
sentences.tr:
keitai par nēessi nekys aklautos athaptos
Patroklos· tou d’ ouk epilēsomai, ophr’ an egōge
zōoisin meteō kai moi phila gounat’ orōrēi·
sentences.i: By the ships lies a dead man, unwept and unburied, Patroclus; and I shall not forget him as long as I am among the living and my own knees move;
sentences.n: κεῖται is ‘lies’, and νέκυς ‘dead man’ is in apposition to Πάτροκλος, which is held back to the next line. ἄκλαυτος and ἄθαπτος are ‘unwept’ and ‘unburied’. τοῦ δ’ οὐκ ἐπιλήσομαι is ‘and I shall not forget him’, with the genitive. ὄφρ’ ἂν … μετέω is a subjunctive of μέτειμι ‘am among’, and φίλα γούνατα is ‘my own knees’, φίλος being possessive; ὀρώρῃ is the perfect subjunctive of ὄρνυμι, ‘are stirring’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ θανόντων περ καταλήθοντ’ εἰν Ἀΐδαο
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ καὶ κεῖθι φίλου μεμνήσομ’ ἑταίρου.
sentences.tr:
ei de thanontōn per katalēthont’ ein Aïdao
autar egō kai keithi philou memnēsom’ hetairou.
sentences.l:
and if indeed they forget the dead in the house of Hades,
yet even there I shall remember my dear companion.
sentences.i: And if, in the house of Hades, they forget the dead, even there I shall remember my dear companion.
sentences.n: The dead in Hades are here imagined as forgetful. καταλήθοντ’ is καταλήθονται, ‘they forget’, with θανόντων ‘the dead’ as its object; the subject is left unspoken. εἰν Ἀΐδαο is ‘in (the house) of Hades’, with ‘house’ understood. αὐτὰρ ἐγώ ‘yet I’ sets Achilles against them, κεῖθι is ‘there’, and μεμνήσομαι is the future of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember’. φίλου ἑταίρου is ‘dear companion’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἄγ’ ἀείδοντες παιήονα κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσι νεώμεθα, τόνδε δ’ ἄγωμεν.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ ag’ aeidontes paiēona kouroi Achaiōn
nēusin epi glaphyrēisi neōmetha, tonde d’ agōmen.
sentences.l:
But now come, singing a paean, young men of the Achaeans,
let us return to the hollow ships, and let us bring this man.
sentences.i: But now come, young men of the Achaeans, singing a paean, let us go back to the hollow ships, and let us bring this man with us.
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ἄγε is ‘but now come’, and ἀείδοντες παιήονα is ‘singing a paean’, a song of triumph and thanks. κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν is ‘young men of the Achaeans’. νεώμεθα is a subjunctive of νέομαι ‘return’, used as an exhortation, and ἄγωμεν likewise ‘let us bring’, with τόνδε ‘this one’ (the body).

sentences.t:
ἠράμεθα μέγα κῦδος· ἐπέφνομεν Ἕκτορα δῖον,
ᾧ Τρῶες κατὰ ἄστυ θεῷ ὣς εὐχετόωντο.
sentences.tr:
ērametha mega kydos· epephnomen Hektora dion,
hōi Trōes kata asty theōi hōs euchetoōnto.
sentences.l:
We have won great glory; we have slain heavenly Hector,
to whom the Trojans through the town prayed as to a god.”
sentences.i: We have won great glory: we have slain heavenly Hector, to whom the Trojans prayed, throughout the town, as to a god.”
sentences.n: ἠράμεθα is the aorist middle of ἄρνυμαι ‘win’, and μέγα κῦδος is ‘great glory’. ἐπέφνομεν is the aorist of φένω ‘slay’, with Ἕκτορα δῖον ‘heavenly Hector’. ᾧ … εὐχετόωντο has the dative of the relative, ‘to whom’; the verb is εὐχετάομαι ‘pray, make vows’ in the imperfect, and θεῷ ὥς is ‘like a god’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα, καὶ Ἕκτορα δῖον ἀεικέα μήδετο ἔργα.
sentences.tr: ē rha, kai Hektora dion aeikea mēdeto erga.
sentences.l: He spoke, and for heavenly Hector devised unseemly deeds.
sentences.i: So he said, and planned unseemly deeds against heavenly Hector.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. μήδετο is the imperfect of μήδομαι ‘plan, devise’, with ἔργα ‘deeds’ and ἀεικέα ‘unseemly’, the same word as in the dishonour done to the body. Ἕκτορα δῖον is the object of ‘devised’ in the sense ‘for/against’.

sentences.t:
ἀμφοτέρων μετόπισθε ποδῶν τέτρηνε τένοντε
ἐς σφυρὸν ἐκ πτέρνης, βοέους δ’ ἐξῆπτεν ἱμάντας,
ἐκ δίφροιο δ’ ἔδησε, κάρη δ’ ἕλκεσθαι ἔασεν·
sentences.tr:
amphoterōn metopisthe podōn tetrēne tenonte
es sphyron ek pternēs, boeous d’ exēpten himantas,
ek diphroio d’ edēse, karē d’ helkesthai easen·
sentences.i: He pierced both tendons at the back of the feet, from heel to ankle, and fastened oxhide straps through them, and tied them to the chariot, and left the head to drag;
sentences.n: τέτρηνε is the aorist of τιτραίνω ‘pierce’, and τένοντε is a dual, ‘the two tendons’; ἀμφοτέρων μετόπισθε ποδῶν is ‘behind (on the back of) both feet’. ἐς σφυρὸν ἐκ πτέρνης is ‘from the heel to the ankle’ (ἐκ ‘from’, ἐς ‘to’). βοέους ἱμάντας are ‘oxhide straps’, and ἐξῆπτεν is the imperfect of ἐξάπτω ‘fasten’; ἔδησε is the aorist of δέω ‘bind’ and ἐκ δίφροιο ‘to the chariot’. κάρη … ἕλκεσθαι ἔασεν is ‘let the head be dragged’, κάρη being the head.

sentences.t:
ἐς δίφρον δ’ ἀναβὰς ἀνά τε κλυτὰ τεύχε’ ἀείρας
μάστιξέν ῥ’ ἐλάαν, τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκοντε πετέσθην.
sentences.tr:
es diphron d’ anabas ana te klyta teuche’ aeiras
mastixen rh’ elaan, tō d’ ouk aekonte petesthēn.
sentences.l:
and having mounted the chariot, and having lifted up the famous armour,
he lashed the horses to drive, and the two, not unwilling, flew.
sentences.i: Then he mounted the chariot, lifted up the famous armour, and lashed the horses to drive; and the two flew on, not unwilling.
sentences.n: ἀναβάς and ἀείρας are aorist participles, ‘having mounted’ and ‘having lifted’, both before the main verb μάστιξεν, ‘lashed’. κλυτά τεύχεα is ‘famous armour’, the armour of Hector (originally Achilles’ own). ῥά is the particle ῥα, and ἐλάαν is the infinitive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’. τὼ is the dual article ‘the two’ (the pair of horses, not named), and ἀέκοντε is the dual of ἀέκων ‘unwilling’; πετέσθην is the dual aorist of πέτομαι ‘fly’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἦν ἑλκομένοιο κονίσαλος, ἀμφὶ δὲ χαῖται
κυάνεαι πίτναντο, κάρη δ’ ἅπαν ἐν κονίῃσι
κεῖτο πάρος χαρίεν·
sentences.tr:
tou d’ ēn helkomenoio konisalos, amphi de chaitai
kyaneai pitnanto, karē d’ hapan en koniēisi
keito paros charien·
sentences.i: As he was dragged a cloud of dust rose from him, and his dark hair spread out on either side, and the whole head, once so graceful, lay in the dust;
sentences.n: τοῦ is Hector, in a genitive ‘from him’, and ἑλκομένοιο is the genitive of the passive participle ‘being dragged’; κονίσαλος is ‘cloud of dust’. χαῖται κυάνεαι are ‘dark hair’, and πίτναντο is the imperfect middle of πίτνημι ‘spread out’; ἀμφί is ‘on both sides’. κάρη ἅπαν ἐν κονίῃσι κεῖτο is ‘the whole head lay in the dust’, and πάρος χαρίεν ‘formerly graceful’ agrees with κάρη. The unit ends at the stop in the middle of line 403.

sentences.t:
τότε δὲ Ζεὺς δυσμενέεσσι
δῶκεν ἀεικίσσασθαι ἑῇ ἐν πατρίδι γαίῃ.
sentences.tr:
tote de Zeus dysmeneessi
dōken aeikissasthai heēi en patridi gaiēi.
sentences.l:
but then Zeus to ill-disposed men
gave to maltreat him in his own native land.
sentences.i: but then Zeus gave it to ill-disposed men to maltreat him in his own native land.
sentences.n: τότε δέ is ‘but then’, set against πάρος ‘formerly’. δυσμενέεσσι is the epic dative plural of δυσμενής ‘ill-disposed’, so ‘to ill-disposed men’, here Hector’s enemies. δῶκεν … ἀεικίσσασθαι is ‘gave (it) to maltreat’, with the infinitive of ἀεικίζω ‘treat unseemly’. ἑῇ is the possessive ‘his own’, and πατρίδι γαίῃ ‘native land’ is Troy; the part ends with the body being dragged away.
